thesis.question: In which recurring ways do listing systems lose liquidity, and what do the failures have in common?
thesis.claim: Listing systems lose liquidity in fifteen recurring patterns, and what they have in common is that each began as a locally reasonable decision under one team's target and that they travel in chains that start at a missing contract, a vanity metric or a hand-off nobody owns.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that each marketplace failure is a separate defect or a single bad decision in the system that showed the symptom, to be fixed there.
thesis.so_what: Faced with a symptom, the reader names the pattern and breaks the chain at its origin, usually with a contract, an owner or a metric definition, instead of funding a downstream fix that will have to be made again.
thesis.how_why: A team that hard-codes the first category tree, accepts a dealer's feed as it is or adds one more ranking boost makes a sensible choice under its own target; the cost is paid later in contacts that never happen, alerts for sold items and scams in the inbox, where no project budget records it. A feed with no contract for absence produces Ghost Inventory downstream, and a vanity metric licenses Multiplier Creep.

supporting_claims.claim: Listing systems lose liquidity through fifteen recurring patterns, each recognizable by observable warning signs, so a team can name the one in front of it.
Each pattern begins as a locally reasonable decision under one team's target, so it is explained by its mechanism (incentives, ownership gaps, missing contracts, the wrong metric), not by blame.
Each pattern's cost lands as lost liquidity, trust, speed and money, far from the project that caused it, and the public record documents that cost where anyone has published it.
The patterns travel in chains that start at a missing contract, a vanity metric or a hand-off nobody owns, so a downstream fix returns unless the chain is broken at its origin.
Each pattern has a remedy direction, a first indicator to measure and chapters that address it, so a reader can go from a named pattern to the place in the book that fixes it.

role.contribution: Gives the book its shared names for failure, so every chapter can open by naming the patterns it works on.

flow.rationale: Each section uses what the one before supplied. The chains need every pattern's name and mechanism; the indicators are read 'with the mechanism in mind' and serve the chains' advice to look upstream; the matrix uses the column codes of names the reader now knows and sits beside the indicators as the second per-pattern reference; the closing habits ask the reader to pair each pattern with its indicator and to look upstream, so they need both. The indicators come before the matrix because they confirm which pattern is active, and the matrix then says where to read about it. With the chains first, the reader would meet fifteen names linked by arrows before knowing any of them; with the matrix before the patterns, its codes would be unreadable.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A category product manager's promise of a new category 'in about six weeks, once search, SEO and the app team have each done their part' shows a delay accepted as normal.

evidence.what: "We can have the new category live in about six weeks..." (a category product manager), with Figure 3: the category tree wired into six consumers while an E-bikes leaf waits six weeks.
evidence.source: Composite quote attributed to a role
evidence.shows: The delay is treated as routine and spread across teams, so no one sees it as a design fault.

advances_thesis.how: Shows The Category Straitjacket as a sensible-sounding statement by one role.

transition_in.introduces: The next pattern, The Category Straitjacket, opened by a role's quote and its figure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In a straitjacketed marketplace category identifiers are hard-coded in every consumer and the tree is not versioned, so a new leaf takes weeks, catch-all leaves grow and country trees drift.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the warning signs of The Category Straitjacket.

transition_in.introduces: What The Category Straitjacket looks like and its observable signs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Hard-coding the first tree was cheap when it rarely changed, but every consumer copied its identifiers and a category is really a schema key, so with no owner of the taxonomy as versioned reference data no one designs change as a migration.

advances_thesis.how: Explains The Category Straitjacket by its mechanism, not by blame.

transition_in.introduces: The incentives and ownership gaps that produce them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Straitjacket costs liquidity, trust, speed and money, and even a well-run marketplace pays heavily for one large re-categorization.

evidence.what: Mercari (2024) re-assigned more than 3 billion items and estimated that LLM labeling of all of them would cost about US$1 million and take about 1.9 years, so it labeled a sample and propagated labels with a nearest-neighbor model.
evidence.shows: A large taxonomy change is a program with a measurable price, even at a well-run marketplace.

advances_thesis.how: Prices The Category Straitjacket and grounds it in the public record.

transition_in.introduces: What it costs, with dated public evidence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Tradeyard's four country trees and six-week lead time make the November 2027 bikes split a large migration, after which a new leaf takes two days.

evidence.what: Four trees of 1,420, 1,380, 980 and 760 leaves; six weeks per category; bikes in 19 leaves with about 640,000 listings; the 1 November 2027 split re-classifies about 410,000 listings, rewrites about 1.3 million saved searches, needs about 2,300 redirects and 2,900 landing pages; Fatbikes added in two days a month later.
evidence.shows: The cost of the hard-coded tree and the payoff of a versioned one, in one brand's numbers.

advances_thesis.how: Shows The Category Straitjacket in the fictional Veldmark group.

transition_in.introduces: A fictional Veldmark illustration with ledger figures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The remedy is to treat the taxonomy as versioned reference data with one owner, referenced by stable identifier, changed through published mappings and a tested migration runbook.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the direction of the remedy for The Category Straitjacket.

transition_in.introduces: The direction of the fix.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five chapters address the Straitjacket: the versioned tree and runbook, attributes tied to categories, query classifiers, the redirect registry and vertical trees.

advances_thesis.how: Points to the chapters that address The Category Straitjacket.

transition_in.introduces: The chapters that carry it out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A feed-integration engineer's 'put it in the extra-fields column for now; we'll clean the data up after launch' shows the shortcut that fills the Junkyard.

evidence.what: "Just put it in the extra-fields column for now..." (a feed-integration engineer), with Figure 4: fuel under four spellings, so a petrol filter finds one car.
evidence.source: Composite quote attributed to a role
evidence.shows: The cleanup is always deferred, and the cost of deferral lands on buyers who filter.

advances_thesis.how: Shows The Attribute Junkyard as a sensible-sounding statement by one role.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapters that address The Category Straitjacket.
transition_in.introduces: The next pattern, The Attribute Junkyard, opened by a role's quote and its figure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In the Junkyard attributes are free-form keys with no attribute dictionary, so one fact arrives under several keys and filters, facets and feeds disagree.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the warning signs of The Attribute Junkyard.

transition_in.introduces: What The Attribute Junkyard looks like and its observable signs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Flexible storage makes a new key free, every team and feed adds its own, a straitjacketed tree pushes new facts into free keys, the channels validate differently, nobody owns the dictionary, and generative assistants now add keys faster than sellers.

advances_thesis.how: Explains The Attribute Junkyard by its mechanism, not by blame.

transition_in.introduces: The incentives and ownership gaps that produce them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Junkyard hides listings from filters and blocks attribute-based rules, and while no marketplace has measured its own junkyard, eBay's public taxonomy API shows what the remedy looks like.

evidence.what: eBay's Taxonomy API publishes per leaf category each aspect's data type, requiredness, controlled or free values, cardinality and an expectedRequiredByDate for new mandatory aspects.
evidence.shows: A governed attribute dictionary is a published, per-category contract, the opposite of free-form keys.

advances_thesis.how: Prices The Attribute Junkyard and grounds it in the public record.

transition_in.introduces: What it costs, with dated public evidence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Tradeyard's 3,900 attribute keys, most of them rarely used, mean a frame-size filter hid three quarters of Dutch bikes.

evidence.what: 3,900 keys in 2026, 41% used on fewer than 0.1% of listings; about 610 worth promoting to typed index fields in 2027; frame size present on 23% of Dutch bike listings before the extraction pilot.
evidence.shows: The Junkyard's cost in one number a buyer feels: three quarters of the inventory invisible to a filter.

advances_thesis.how: Shows The Attribute Junkyard in the fictional Veldmark group.

transition_in.introduces: A fictional Veldmark illustration with ledger figures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The remedy is one attribute dictionary per vertical, the same validation on every channel, provenance on every value, and deliberate promotion and retirement of keys.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the direction of the remedy for The Attribute Junkyard.

transition_in.introduces: The direction of the fix.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five chapters address the Junkyard: the dictionary, normalization with provenance, category-scoped schemas, typed index fields and constrained AI assistants.

advances_thesis.how: Points to the chapters that address The Attribute Junkyard.

transition_in.introduces: The chapters that carry it out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A listing-service engineer's 'It's marked sold in the database. Whatever the alert e-mail said this morning isn't our service' shows that each team owns only its own copy.

evidence.what: "It's marked sold in the database..." (a listing-service engineer), with Figure 5: Femke's bike leaves search a minute after it sells but goes to 214 users in the next morning's digest.
evidence.source: Composite quote attributed to a role
evidence.shows: Removal is correct at the source and wrong in the copies nobody owns.

advances_thesis.how: Shows Ghost Inventory as a sensible-sounding statement by one role.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapters that address The Attribute Junkyard.
transition_in.introduces: The next pattern, Ghost Inventory, opened by a role's quote and its figure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ghost Inventory is sold, expired or removed listings that stay visible in search, carousels, alert digests, caches, SEO pages, partner feeds and contact buttons, and nobody can state removal latency beyond the search index.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the warning signs of Ghost Inventory.

transition_in.introduces: What Ghost Inventory looks like and its observable signs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Removal is the change teams design least: publication gets a pipeline and a target, unpublication gets a flag, each consumer copies state on its own schedule, feeds omit deletes and offline sellers never mark items sold.

advances_thesis.how: Explains Ghost Inventory by its mechanism, not by blame.

transition_in.introduces: The incentives and ownership gaps that produce them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ghosts waste contacts and alerts, look like scams and charge professionals for dead leads, and although no marketplace publishes a ghost rate, downstream channels already punish staleness.

evidence.what: Google's job-posting guidance: "Failure to take timely action on expired jobs may result in a manual action".
evidence.shows: A search engine penalizes stale listings, so ghosts cost traffic as well as trust.

evidence.what: Google Merchant Center expires product data 30 days after its last refresh.
evidence.shows: Downstream channels enforce freshness the marketplace itself may not.

advances_thesis.how: Prices Ghost Inventory and grounds it in the public record.

transition_in.introduces: What it costs, with dated public evidence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Femke's bike, listed on a Sunday evening and sold the next day, is removed from search within a minute yet still reaches 214 users the next morning, and an audit finds about 41,000 Dutch ghosts a week.

evidence.what: Listed on the evening of Sunday 7 March 2027; sold on Monday 8 March 2027 at 18:10, removed from search at 18:11; a digest built at 17:30 from a replica snapshot goes to 214 users at 07:00 on Tuesday; about 41,000 Dutch listings a week still in a downstream copy 24 hours after ending; at Motorvane the Essen Golf's removal arrives 26 hours late and three enquiries arrive in between.
evidence.shows: Removal can be fast at the source and slow in every copy that does not listen for it.

advances_thesis.how: Shows Ghost Inventory in the fictional Veldmark group.

transition_in.introduces: A fictional Veldmark illustration with ledger figures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The remedy is to make removal a lifecycle event with a latency objective per registered consumer, re-check availability at send time, reconcile feeds and serve correct status codes for gone pages.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the direction of the remedy for Ghost Inventory.

transition_in.introduces: The direction of the fix.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Seven chapters address Ghost Inventory, from removal objectives and ordered events to staleness budgets on read models (copies of listing data shaped for one consumer), alert re-checks, feed reconciliation, gone pages and serving-time filters.

advances_thesis.how: Points to the chapters that address Ghost Inventory.

transition_in.introduces: The chapters that carry it out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A real-estate product owner's 'Three agencies hold the mandate, so three listings is correct. Isn't it?' shows a duplicate defended as correct.

evidence.what: "Three agencies hold the mandate..." (a real-estate portal product owner), with Figure 6: one Lyon flat at €389,000 arriving three times and stacking three pins on one building.
evidence.source: Composite quote attributed to a role
evidence.shows: Duplicates feel legitimate to the people who produce them.

advances_thesis.how: Shows Seeing Double as a sensible-sounding statement by one role.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapters that address Ghost Inventory.
transition_in.introduces: The next pattern, Seeing Double, opened by a role's quote and its figure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Seeing Double is the same item or property appearing many times, from reposts, two channels, several agencies holding a mandate, or stolen photos.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the warning signs of Seeing Double.

transition_in.introduces: What Seeing Double looks like and its observable signs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Duplicates are rewarded, feeds lack stable keys, and nobody owns showing a thing once because deduplication looks cosmetic rather than like entity resolution, with abusive and legitimate duplicates mixed up.

advances_thesis.how: Explains Seeing Double by its mechanism, not by blame.

transition_in.introduces: The incentives and ownership gaps that produce them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Duplicates split demand, inflate supply, hide fakes and multiply processing, and property portals productize the presentation problem.

evidence.what: In 2021 Idealista launched a duplicate-control tool that groups listings of one property, including those on other portals, and notifies users of price changes, removals and new duplicates (trade-press report).
evidence.shows: Duplicates are common enough in property that a portal built a product to manage them.

advances_thesis.how: Prices Seeing Double and grounds it in the public record.

transition_in.introduces: What it costs, with dated public evidence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Hearthly France has 1.7 listings per property, one Lyon flat arrives three times, and photo-match alerts on stolen photos are closed as legitimate duplicates.

evidence.what: 1.9 million listings for about 1.12 million properties in 2026; a 68 m² Lyon flat at €389,000 from three agencies through two vendors and Keybridge in May 2027; 11 photo-match alerts in the Barcelona ring closed as legitimate duplicates.
evidence.shows: Legitimate and abusive duplicates look alike until someone owns the difference.

advances_thesis.how: Shows Seeing Double in the fictional Veldmark group.

transition_in.introduces: A fictional Veldmark illustration with ledger figures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The remedy is to separate abusive duplicates, which go to enforcement, from legitimate ones, which are clustered and shown once, with cluster identity kept outside the index and the representative chosen by quality.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the direction of the remedy for Seeing Double.

transition_in.introduces: The direction of the fix.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Six chapters address Seeing Double: matching and clustering, perceptual hashes, precise location, repeated partner records, map clustering and stolen photos as fraud.

advances_thesis.how: Points to the chapters that address Seeing Double.

transition_in.introduces: The chapters that carry it out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An on-call engineer's 'The dealer's file looked fine last night. We'll find out what happened when support opens' shows that nobody checks a feed before it changes live stock.

evidence.what: "The dealer's file looked fine last night..." (an ingestion on-call engineer), with Figure 7: a truncated file unpublishing 38,400 Motorvane listings at 02:40.
evidence.source: Composite quote attributed to a role
evidence.shows: Feeds are trusted until the partner's customers report the damage.

advances_thesis.how: Shows Feed Roulette as a sensible-sounding statement by one role.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapters that address Seeing Double.
transition_in.introduces: The next pattern, Feed Roulette, opened by a role's quote and its figure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Feed Roulette is ingesting professional and partner feeds without a feed contract, so records skip validation, writes are not idempotent, partners get no error report and nothing guards a truncated file.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the warning signs of Feed Roulette.

transition_in.introduces: What Feed Roulette looks like and its observable signs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Feeds are integrated one partner at a time as code adapters, rejecting a paying customer's data feels risky, full snapshots are easy and dangerous, error reporting has no owner and vendors do the minimum.

advances_thesis.how: Explains Feed Roulette by its mechanism, not by blame.

transition_in.introduces: The incentives and ownership gaps that produce them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Feed Roulette loses the professional stock that is most of the supply in automotive and real estate, and because dealers multi-home, lost confidence moves stock to competitors; public partner APIs show the remedy.

evidence.what: Bundeskartellamt (2026): "many platforms offer dealers data export to other platforms"; dealer multi-homing treated as a competitive constraint.
evidence.shows: A dealer who loses confidence in one platform's feed can shift attention to another.

evidence.what: mobile.de's Seller API makes creation idempotent through an insertion request ID, answers a retry with 303 to the existing ad, and returns stable error keys; RFC 9457 standardizes problem details.
evidence.source: mobile.de Seller API documentation, n.d.; IETF, 2023
evidence.shows: A feed contract with idempotency and machine-readable errors exists in public practice.

advances_thesis.how: Prices Feed Roulette and grounds it in the public record.

transition_in.introduces: What it costs, with dated public evidence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Truncated files for 286 Motorvane dealers unpublish 38,400 listings overnight, a fifth return with new identifiers, and a few Hearthly vendors cause most incidents.

evidence.what: Monday 8 March 2027, 02:40 CET: files for 286 dealers; 38,400 listings unpublished by 02:55, about 1,900 with paid top placements; complete files at 09:40; a fifth back with new identifiers; more than 600 support calls; about 30 of 160 Hearthly vendors cause most incidents.
evidence.shows: One unguarded snapshot damages stock, paid placements and identifiers at once.

advances_thesis.how: Shows Feed Roulette in the fictional Veldmark group.

transition_in.introduces: A fictional Veldmark illustration with ledger figures.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The remedy is a contract for every channel: an envelope, schema versions, stable error codes, per-run reports, stable keys, a mass-change guard and reconciliation.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the direction of the remedy for Feed Roulette.

transition_in.introduces: The direction of the fix.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five chapters address Feed Roulette: feed contracts and guards, shared validation, integration partners, partner error views and automotive dealer APIs.

advances_thesis.how: Points to the chapters that address Feed Roulette.

transition_in.introduces: The chapters that carry it out.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A search engineer's 'Don't touch the Solr collection. Some of those fields only exist there' shows an index that has become the only copy.

evidence.what: "Don't touch the Solr collection..." (a search engineer), with Figure 8: teams writing counters and fixes into Solr, and a Sunday reindex pushing p99 latency to about 7 seconds.
evidence.source: Composite quote attributed to a role
evidence.shows: The index holds data nothing else holds, so it cannot be rebuilt safely.

advances_thesis.how: Shows Search as System of Record as a sensible-sounding statement by one role.

transition_in.carries_over: The chapters that address Feed Roulette.
transition_in.introduces: The next pattern, Search as System of Record, opened by a role's quote and its figure.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A system of record is the one authoritative copy from which other copies are rebuilt; when search becomes it, the index holds data that exists nowhere else, 'published' means 'in the index', other services query it, and a rebuild is an event or impossible.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the warning signs of Search as System of Record.

transition_in.introduces: What Search as System of Record looks like and its observable signs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The index is the fastest complete view, so teams write counters, enrichment, flags and fixes into it directly, skipping the system of record, and no event stream carries enough to rebuild it.

advances_thesis.how: Explains Search as System of Record by its mechanism, not by blame.

transition_in.introduces: The incentives and ownership gaps that produce them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: An index that cannot be rebuilt degrades search at peaks, cannot explain missing listings and blocks schema and engine change, while rebuilding from an event stream is a documented alternative.

conclusion.heading: Using the Patterns
conclusion.synthesis: The fifteen patterns are one failure seen fifteen times: variation that accumulated under separate targets instead of being decided, owned and measured; the remedy is the same in each case, a contract, an owner or a metric definition placed at the origin of the chain.
conclusion.so_what: A reader facing a symptom can name the pattern, ask for its indicator and fund the upstream fix instead of a downstream one that will have to be made again.

callback.how: The last paragraph names them as Ghost Inventory, Seeing Double, Feed Roulette and Multiplier Creep, each with an upstream cause.

takeaway.content: Use the names in design reviews, steering committees and portfolio reviews: name the mechanism, pair it with a measure and look upstream first.
